newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian banks seen cutting rates but in small doses.
newsitem.headline: Indian banks seen cutting rates but in small doses.

text.p: Commercial banks were likely to answer the Reserve Bank of India's one percentage cut in its bank rate with smaller cuts in their prime lending rates, analysts said on Wednesday.
The RBI earlier announced it had cut the bank rate, the rate at which banks borrow from the central bank, to 10 percent per annum from 11 percent with immediate effect.
The move was seen as a signal to banks to reduce lending rates and aid a recovery in industrial growth.

Two years ago controlling inflation was India's priority but the consequent high interest rates were a major factor leading to a slowdown in industrial growth in the second half of 1996/97 (April-March).
Analysts said banks were likely to cut prime rates but reductions would be small as they sought to protect spreads.
"I think banks will follow (the RBI's move) and cut (prime rates) by 50 to 100 basis points, more likely by 50," said Tabassum Inamdar, banking analyst at Jardine Fleming (India) Broking.
Analysts said banks' decisions to cut interest rates, in an effort to boost poor loan disbursals, would be tempered by past experience.
Banks cut prime lending rates by 150-200 basis points last year in response to complaints from borrowers over the high cost of funds and RBI measures to reduce interest rates.
But the interest rate cuts failed to fuel credit demand.

While bank deposits have grown by 141.12 billion rupees ($3.94 billion) over the end-March figure to 5,177.07 billion, loans have grown by only 11.41 billion to 2,776.71 billion so far in the current financial year (April-March).
"The real question is whether interest rates are standing in the way of credit offtake," said S.R. Krishnan, banking analyst at Peregrine Capital India.

"Despite a prime rate of 14.0 percent and commercial paper at 9.0-10.0 percent, there is no real demand for credit," Krishnan said. Analysts said deposit rates would also have to be cut to avoid a squeeze on bank spreads.
"Without a deposit rate cut, banks cannot cut prime lending rates," Krishan said. "Banks' margins will be squeezed further."
The RBI has ordered maximum rates on deposits up to one year should be reduced to eight percent from nine percent per annum.
"On the deposit side they have to cut by 100 basis points for deposits up to one year, and on longer term deposits the banks may choose to cut by less," Inamdar said.
